I am 65 years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou for 40 years. My back is not what it used to be, but I know every inch of these 9 mu. With seven mouths to feed and some of the younger ones working in Shijiazhuang or Handan, I must grow enough grain to feed the household and keep some cotton for cash. I will not try anything new or risky—at my age, steady and familiar is better.

I will put 6 mu into my wheat-maize rotation, which is the backbone of our food supply. Wheat will go in this autumn as usual. I will buy improved wheat seed from the township shop; I do not save my own seed anymore because the yield drops. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as a base and top-dress with urea in spring—about 25 kg of nitrogen, 8 kg of phosphate, and 5 kg of potassium per mu. The soil here still has some strength, so I do not overdo it. I will irrigate three times from my well: once before winter to protect the seedlings, once at jointing, and once at heading if the spring is dry. That is enough; electricity for the pump costs money. I will do rotary tillage before sowing because it is easier on my bones than deep plowing. If the weather is fair, I expect about 500 kg per mu.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid maize on the same 6 mu. Everyone knows you must buy hybrid corn seed fresh each year; saved seed is a waste of land. I will use less fertilizer than wheat—about 20 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu—and irrigate twice, at jointing and at tasseling, unless the summer rains are good. Two pesticide sprays: one for weeds at planting, and one for corn borer if I see them in the field. Quick rotary tillage after wheat harvest, then sow without delay. I should get around 550 kg per mu.

The remaining 3 mu I will plant to cotton in late April. Cotton is hard work—especially the picking in autumn when my fingers ache and my back hurts—but it brings in cash, which we need for daily expenses and for my grandchildren’s school fees. I will buy hybrid cotton seed. Cotton needs more potassium than grain, so I will put down about 18 kg nitrogen, 8 kg phosphorus, and 10 kg potassium per mu. I will plough that field in spring to warm the soil, because cotton likes loose, warm earth. I will irrigate three times during flowering and boll-setting, and I must spray four times for bollworm and aphids—cotton always attracts pests. With my daughter-in-law helping pick in autumn, I hope for 280 kg of seed cotton per mu. That is my plan.
